description: Hastings, castle-building and the feudal levy — Norman conquest and its impact on English society.
content_html:
The Battle of Hastings and Norman Conquest

On 14 October 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings. Harold was killed — traditionally said to have been struck by an arrow — and the English army collapsed. William marched to London and was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. The Norman Conquest was one of the most transformative events in English history, replacing the Anglo-Saxon ruling class with Norman lords almost entirely within a generation.

English resistance did not collapse immediately. The north of England rose repeatedly in 1067–70. In 1069, a Danish fleet landed in support of the northern rebels, and William responded with the devastating Harrying of the North. Contemporary accounts describe mass death from starvation and cold across Yorkshire. Chronicler Orderic Vitalis, writing in the early twelfth century, described the land lying uncultivated for nine years and thousands of bodies left to rot. Historians continue to debate the scale of the destruction, but Domesday Book (1086) records large areas of Yorkshire as “waste,” confirming long-term depopulation.

Key Fact

William I’s Harrying of the North (1069–70) was a deliberate scorched-earth campaign to crush northern resistance. Domesday Book (1086) records extensive areas of Yorkshire as “waste,” suggesting lasting depopulation and economic destruction.

Castle-Building and Military Control

The Normans used castles as instruments of conquest and control. The earliest were motte-and-bailey castles: quick to build using forced local labour and highly effective as garrison points. Within a decade of 1066, hundreds had been built across England. Some, like the Tower of London, were rebuilt in stone as permanent symbols of Norman power.

Castles served multiple functions: they housed garrisons to suppress rebellion, provided bases for rapid military response, and demonstrated the physical dominance of Norman lords over the surrounding population. They also disrupted existing communities — in some towns, houses were demolished to make way for castle construction. The castle-building programme was funded partly through the feudal system.

The Norman feudal system reorganised English society around military obligation. The king held all land and granted it to tenants-in-chief (great barons and bishops) in exchange for knight service — the provision of armed knights for royal campaigns. Barons sublet land to knights, who in turn held peasant farmers (villeins) who worked the land and owed labour services.

The Domesday Book of 1086 recorded all landownership in England, allowing William to assess who held land, how much military service they owed and what taxes could be raised. It was the most detailed administrative survey in medieval Europe and gave the Crown an unprecedented picture of its resources.

Feudal Breakdown: Stephen and The Anarchy

The feudal system depended on a strong king keeping barons loyal through a mixture of reward and force. When Henry I died in 1135 without a male heir, England plunged into civil war between his daughter, Empress Matilda, and his nephew, Stephen. The period 1135–54 is known as The Anarchy because of the breakdown of royal authority.

Contemporary chronicler the “Peterborough Chronicler” described barons building unlicensed castles and oppressing the common people with impunity — “it was said openly that Christ and his saints slept.” The civil war demonstrated a fundamental weakness in the feudal system: when competing claimants each sought baronial support by granting concessions, central authority collapsed and lords acted as local warlords. Order was only restored when Stephen agreed the Treaty of Wallingford (1153), recognising Matilda’s son Henry as his heir.

A second major feudal breakdown came under King John (1199–1216). John lost Normandy to France at the Battle of Bouvines (1214), making him deeply unpopular with barons who had estates on both sides of the Channel. His demands for money — through scutage (a tax in place of military service) and arbitrary fines — broke the feudal compact. In 1215, barons forced John to sign Magna Carta, which placed limits on royal taxation and arbitrary imprisonment.

John repudiated Magna Carta almost immediately. The First Barons’ War (1215–17) followed, with rebel barons inviting the French prince Louis to claim the English throne. John’s death in 1216 changed the situation: his nine-year-old son Henry III reissued Magna Carta as a peace offering, and the regent William Marshal defeated the French at the Battle of Lincoln (1217), ending the war. Magna Carta survived as a foundation document limiting royal power.

Key Fact

The feudal system was built on the relationship between king and barons. When that relationship broke down — through disputed succession (The Anarchy) or royal overreach (John) — the same barons who were supposed to provide military service instead turned their forces against the Crown.
exam_tip_html: For Explain Why questions on the Norman Conquest, avoid simply listing facts about Hastings. Instead, link your reasons to consequences: explain why castle-building was effective (speed, garrison function, psychological impact on locals), and why the feudal system contained the seeds of future instability (baron power, succession crises). For Change and Continuity essays covering this period, note that while military methods changed dramatically (from fyrd-based Anglo-Saxon warfare to professional knight service), the basic challenge of keeping powerful landowners loyal to the Crown remained constant.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Norman Conquest (1066) transformed England through military conquest, the Harrying of the North, and systematic castle-building that imposed Norman authority on a resistant population.
  • The feudal system created a military hierarchy with the king at the top, but it depended on a strong monarch — as The Anarchy (1135–54) and the First Barons’ War (1215–17) showed when royal authority weakened.
  • Magna Carta (1215) was the most lasting consequence of feudal breakdown under John — a document that survived to limit royal power across the centuries.

practice_questions.text: Give one reason why William I used castles to control England after 1066.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: precise feature with accurate supporting detail (e.g. motte-and-bailey castles could be built quickly using forced labour, allowing rapid establishment of Norman garrisons). Developing: vague (e.g. 'they were strong buildings').

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the feudal system introduced by the Normans.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for accurate supporting detail). Mastering: e.g. king grants land to tenants-in-chief in exchange for knight service; barons sublet to knights in exchange for military obligation. Developing: identifies features without supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Harrying of the North (1069–70) was significant in establishing Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — links military effectiveness (destroyed northern resistance), economic impact (Domesday evidence of 'waste'), and psychological deterrence (future risings suppressed by example). Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence — explains significance with accurate detail across two or more reasons. Developing: Some argument with basic evidence. Emerging: Simple points; evidence limited or missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the feudal system sometimes broke down in the period 1066–1215.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers disputed succession (The Anarchy 1135), weak king unable to enforce obligations (John), and how barons exploited weakness for their own gain; links to Magna Carta as outcome. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did the Norman Conquest change the lives of ordinary people in England? Explain your answer using evidence from the period 1066–1215.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — balanced essay covering changed lives (Harrying, castle construction destroying homes, villeinage, replacement of Anglo-Saxon lords) and elements of continuity (farming patterns, basic village structure, Christian church) with a sustained evidenced judgement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence and sustained explanation. Developing: Some argument with basic evidence, mostly one-sided. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Magna Carta (1215) was an important consequence of the breakdown of the feudal relationship between king and barons.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — links John's specific violations of feudal compact (scutage, arbitrary fines, loss of Normandy), explains how this motivated barons to act collectively, and analyses Magna Carta's significance as a limit on royal power. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the Harrying of the North?
options: A Viking raid on Northumberland in 1066
William I's campaign of destruction across northern England in 1069–70
A baronial rebellion against Stephen in 1140
A Danish invasion repelled by Harold Godwinson

knowledge_checks.q: Which document from 1086 recorded landownership across England, allowing William I to assess military and tax obligations?
The period 1135–54, when England was torn by civil war between Empress Matilda and Stephen, is known as _____.
In 1215, rebel barons forced King John to sign _____, which placed limits on royal taxation and arbitrary imprisonment.
Match each Norman period term with its meaning:
right: great lords who held land directly from the king
early Norman castle with earthwork mound and courtyard
a tax paid instead of providing military service

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Battle of Hastings?
What was the Harrying of the North?
flashcard_questions.a: William I's destruction of settlements and food supplies in Yorkshire, 1069–70
All landownership in England, including military obligations and taxes owed to the Crown
A quick-build Norman castle with a raised earthwork mound topped by a tower, connected to an enclosed courtyard
A hierarchy in which the king granted land to barons in exchange for military service
A civil war between Empress Matilda and Stephen that caused a breakdown in royal authority
King John's arbitrary taxation and loss of Normandy at Bouvines (1214) turned barons against him
A charter of rights (1215) placing limits on royal power and establishing that the king was subject to law
A tax paid in place of military service under the feudal system

flashcard_questions.q: Who won the First Barons' War and what ended it?
flashcard_questions.a: Henry III's forces under regent William Marshal; ended by Henry III reissuing Magna Carta

glossary_terms.definition: William I's systematic destruction of settlements, livestock and food supplies across Yorkshire and the north of England in 1069–70, killing thousands and leaving the region waste for years.
An early Norman castle design with a raised earthwork mound (motte) topped by a wooden tower, connected to an enclosed courtyard (bailey).
The hierarchical system of land tenure in medieval England, in which the king granted land to barons in exchange for military service, who in turn sublet to knights and lesser tenants.
Great lords who held land directly from the king in exchange for military service and counsel.
A charter of rights agreed in 1215 between King John and rebel barons, limiting royal power and establishing that the king was subject to the law.
